newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee could climb over $2.00 --Merrill Lynch.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee could climb over $2.00 --Merrill Lynch.

text.p: Tight supplies of high-quality arabica coffee and continued dry weather in Central America could propel coffee futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) well over the $2 per lb level, U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch said.

"The coffee market seems to be adhering to the seasonal patterns, where the market makes its lows in mid-July and then rallies thereafter," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes in a bi-weekly report dated July 31. "The rebound this season could even be stronger than in prior years as never before have quality supplies been as lean ahead of the new crop harvest as they are this year."
She added: "We anticipate the market climbing over $2.00 and could rally back to as much as $2.30-$2.50, if not higher if the weather (in Central America) remains dry."

Ganes said concerns were growing that dry conditions in Central America could adversely affect the 1997/98 coffee crop. She said sources in El Salvador suggested that the crop will fall short of the USDA June estimate of 2.59 million 60-kg bags and that the quality of the beans could be reduced.
However, forecaster Cropcast noted in its daily weather update on Friday that Central American coffee areas have had light to moderate rainfall during the past week.
"This precipitation helped to reinforce moisture supplies in the region, following some drier conditions in the area during the past few weeks," Cropcast said.

Merrill Lynch's Ganes also noted that aggressive shipments earlier this year by many Central American producers mean there is very little coffee remaining to bridge the gap between the 1996/97 and 1997/98 harvests.
Additionally, much of the coffee that has made its way to the U.S. recently has been less desirable, poorer quality beans, she said.

"While certified and non-certified coffee U.S. stocks have been rising in recent months, lending an appearance of a more amply supplied market, in reality much of the build was in lower quality African coffee, Brazilians and robustas," she said. "Large quantities of better quality coffee simply will not be available until at least November."
Ganes said sources in second-leading producer Colombia suggested the country's new-crop harvest will be delayed by six-to-eight weeks and might not be available until December.

"As a result, the existing supplies of coffee will need to be stretched that much further," Ganes said. "The market is beginning to respond to this with the September contract now approaching $2.00 and reaching the level where the July contract had expired."
On Friday, CSCE's September contract ended 0.45 cent per lb higher at 184.95 cents.
